title: Why Growing Businesses Are Replacing Their Agency With a Small Freelance Team
author: Buzz Tum
contentHtml:
Why Growing Businesses Are Quietly Replacing Their Agency With a Small Freelance Team

There's a specific moment a lot of business owners hit. The agency invoice lands, the monthly report goes out, and you read it twice trying to figure out what, exactly, you got for the money. Nothing on the page is wrong. It's just not enough.

That feeling isn't new, and it isn't rare. What's changed is what businesses are doing about it.

The Agency Model Was Built for a Different Era

Retainers made sense when hiring specialists individually meant job postings, interviews, payroll, and months of ramp-up. An agency packaged all of that into one invoice. For a long time, that trade-off was worth it.

The problem is that the package didn't shrink as the work got more specific. You're still paying a blended rate that covers account managers, junior staff rotation, and overhead you never see. Meanwhile, the actual work, the SEO strategy, the code, the day-to-day admin, gets handled by whoever's available that week.

If you want a clearer picture of what this looks like in practice, this rundown of the warning signs your agency retainer isn't earning its keep walks through it well. It's the kind of thing that's obvious once someone points it out, and almost invisible until then.

What Changes When One Person Owns the Work

Here's the shift that actually matters. When you hire a freelancer for a specific job, there's no handoff. The person who quoted you the work is the person doing it, and the person doing it is the person you talk to when something needs adjusting.

That sounds small. It isn't.

A change that would take an agency a week of scoping and sign-off can happen in a single conversation. You're not waiting on a process. You're talking to the person who can just fix it.

This piece on the case for hiring a freelancer instead of an agency goes deeper into why this shift in accountability changes the relationship entirely, not just the price.

The Three Roles Most Small Businesses Actually Need

Most businesses don't need ten specialists. They need three, and they need them to be good.

The first is someone who understands search the way engines actually read it now: entities, topical relationships, and site structure, not just keyword density. An SEO consultant who works this way builds visibility that compounds, instead of chasing rankings that move every algorithm update.

The second is someone on the technical side. Whether that's fixing a slow checkout page, rebuilding a site that hasn't been touched since 2019, or making sure your SEO work has a fast, clean foundation to actually rank on, web development is where strategy either becomes real or quietly dies in a ticket queue.

The third role gets overlooked the most, and it's often the one that frees up the most time. A virtual assistant handling inbox management, scheduling, research, and the dozens of small recurring tasks that eat a founder's week isn't a luxury. It's usually the difference between a business owner working on the business and one stuck working in it.

You don't need to hire all three at once. Most businesses build this team one piece at a time, starting with whichever gap is costing them the most right now. The full range of services covers each of these areas individually, so you can bring people in as the need becomes obvious rather than all at once.

Publishing More Isn't the Same as Being Found

Here's something worth sitting with for a second, because it trips up a lot of businesses that are otherwise doing everything right.

Content volume and visibility are not the same thing. A business can publish three articles a week for a year and see almost no movement in qualified traffic, while a competitor publishing half as often gets found consistently for the exact searches that matter. The difference usually comes down to whether the content was built around what people are actually searching for, or just around a calendar.

This breakdown on publishing more versus getting discovered covers the distinction in more detail, and it's relevant whether you're working with a content team, a single writer, or doing it yourself between everything else.

What This Actually Looks Like for a Typical Business

A business with a website that hasn't changed much in a few years, some organic traffic that's flat or slowly declining, and a founder who's personally answering most of the emails that come in. That's a common starting point, and it's worth describing because it doesn't look like a crisis. It looks like Tuesday.

The SEO work usually starts with an audit, not a content calendar. What's already ranking, what's close to ranking, and what's structurally broken on the site itself. The web development side often comes in here too, because half the time the SEO recommendations and the technical fixes are the same conversation.

The admin side tends to get added a few weeks later, once the founder realizes they've spent an afternoon on calendar tetris instead of the work only they can do.

None of this requires a transformation. It's just three people, each doing one thing well, working from the same understanding of the business.

Making the Switch Without the Risk

You don't have to cancel an agency contract on a Friday and figure out the rest over the weekend. Most businesses run a freelance specialist alongside their existing setup for a month or two, just to see the difference in turnaround and communication firsthand.

Start with whichever role is costing you the most right now. If your site hasn't moved in search results in over a year, that's usually the SEO consultant. If your site is the thing slowing everything else down, start with web development. If you're the bottleneck on your own calendar, a virtual assistant pays for itself faster than almost anything else you could hire for.

Get in touch and walk through where things stand. No retainer required to start the conversation, and no pressure to restructure your entire setup on day one. Sometimes the fix really is just one person, doing one thing, well.
